title: Building mSeat: How We Engineered a 1-Click MBBS Mock Counselling Engine for 18,000+ Telangana NEET Aspirants
excerpt: What started as a simple marks-to-rank estimator collapsed under real NEET-UG variance, forcing a full rewrite into a seat-allocation engine for 18,000+ aspirants and 6,000+ MBBS seats. This is the story of the failures, the data model, the UI simplification, and why MCP became the clean escape hatch for AI-assisted counseling.
content:
We were wrong in the first week, wrong in the first model, and wrong in the first architecture. That’s the honest version of how mSeat started: not as a polished counseling product, but as a small attempt to answer one question students kept asking in every possible variation — “Given my rank, what will I actually get?”

What followed was a very technical reminder that admissions counseling is not a simple ranking problem. It’s a combinatorial allocation problem, a data integrity problem, a UX problem, and, at times, a humility problem. The more we built, the more we discovered that the real challenge was not prediction — it was modeling the rules without lying to users.

Phase 1: The rank predictor that failed spectacularly

The original idea was embarrassingly simple: estimate marks, map marks to rank, and use last year’s cutoffs to suggest colleges. I even added a slider to “adjust” for paper difficulty because it felt clever at the time. It wasn’t.

Then the real results came in. The model was off by around 1 lakh ranks for my niece. That wasn’t a small calibration error — it was a complete failure of the mental model. Score inflation had broken every linear assumption I had made. The app wasn’t slightly inaccurate; it was structurally untrustworthy.

  • What I assumed: marks and rank would move roughly linearly.
  • What happened: the distribution shifted hard enough to invalidate the model.
  • Lesson: if the input distribution is unstable, the predictor is not a predictor — it’s a guess with a UI.

That failure forced the first pivot: stop trying to predict rank from marks alone. Predict the seat allocation outcome instead.

Phase 2: The reverse-engineering trap

Once I pivoted to seat prediction, I thought I had the problem under control. I took last year’s seats, ranks, and marks, added the newly announced seats, and wrote the first version of the app. It looked good on paper. It even looked good in the browser.

But it had a hidden flaw: I had reverse-engineered the logic using only one category. That worked until it didn’t. The moment the same logic hit SC, ST, BC, EWS, women horizontal reservation, and domicile rules, the whole thing started over-allocating colleges. It was showing eligibility where none existed.

That’s when it became obvious that Telangana medical counseling is not a single ranking table. It is a 7-dimensional combinatorial matrix:

  • Statewide merit rank across 18,000+ candidates
  • Micro-category quotas like SC-1, SC-2, SC-3, ST, BC-A/B/C/D/E, EWS, OC
  • Horizontal reservation for women
  • 85% local vs 15% unreserved domicile logic
  • Newly added MBBS seats for the current admission cycle
  • Human behavior at the top of the merit list
  • Seat migration caused by AIQ choices and category spillover

At that point, the problem stopped being “can we estimate?” and became “can we simulate the official allocation rules closely enough that families can trust the result?”

Phase 3: The architecture that finally made sense

Once the logic stabilized, the system evolved into a browser-first simulator with an AI-assisted layer on top. The goal was zero friction: enter a rank, get a result, no 15-field form, no paywall, no scavenger hunt through old spreadsheets.

graph TD
    A[User Input: AIR or State Rank] --> B{Merit List Engine}
    B -->|State Rank Found in 18,000+ Dataset| C[Auto-Populate AIR, Score, Category, Gender]
    B -->|Manual User Override| D[Adopt User-Selected Category and Quotas]
    
    C --> E[Compute Cumulative Category Rank in O(1) Time]
    D --> E
    
    E --> F[Preference Engine: 59 Colleges Ordered by Distance from Rajendranagar]
    F --> G[Eligibility Evaluator: CatRank <= College Closing Rank]
    
    G --> H{Allocation Outcome}
    H -->|Eligible| I[Allocated College Card, Safety Margin and Alternatives]
    H -->|Borderline / Not Clear| J[Mop-Up Guidance and Borderline Possibilities]
    
    K[Natural Language Query] --> L[AI Counselor Intent Classifier]
    L --> M[Fees / Documents / College Info or Probability]

The important part here is not the diagram itself. It’s the fact that the engine had to be deterministic where it mattered and flexible where users expected exploration. The app had to answer “what do I get?” and also “what if I pretend I’m in another quota?” without corrupting the real profile.

Phase 4: The hard engineering problems underneath the UI

The UI looked simple. The implementation absolutely was not.

1) O(1) cumulative category rank resolution

Users don’t just need general rank. They need category rank, and they need it instantly. A naive scan on every input change made the interface stutter. So we built an in-memory cumulative index on page load, allowing the app to compute category rank in constant time.

CategoryRank(StateRank, Category) became a direct lookup instead of a loop. That small change turned the app from sluggish to immediate.

2) Non-monotonic score inversion

During calibration, some scores looked wrong by a point or two. At first I thought it was a bad interpolation formula. It turned out the merit list itself contained out-of-order anomalies caused by special weightages like NCC or sports. Those candidates could appear far away from peers with the same raw score.

The fix was not to force a smooth line over bad data. The fix was to stop pretending the data was smooth. We used median monotonic curve filtering and direct rank lookups for known entries, which eliminated the bad interpolation artifacts.

3) Manual override vs auto-detection

One of the most annoying bugs was also one of the easiest to miss. A user would enter a rank, the app would auto-detect the official category, and then an advanced user would try a “what if” scenario — only for the auto-detection to overwrite their choice.

The final behavior was stateful and explicit:

  • Auto-discovery by default when a rank is entered
  • User override lock once someone manually changes the category
  • Category-specific cutoff evaluation for each simulated scenario

4) Killing a 5.8 MB payload

The dataset originally shipped as a giant JSON blob. On mobile, that was a disaster. The app would load before the dataset finished fetching, and the one-click button would appear dead. The problem wasn’t logic — it was payload size and network timing.

We compressed the representation into compact primitive arrays:

// Format: [stateRank, air, score, rawCategory, gender, isEWS]
const rawMeritData = [
  [1, 1420, 695, "OC", "M", 0],
  ...
  [8367, 289635, 393, "SC2", "F", 0],
  ...
  [18602, 1205432, 113, "BCB", "M", 0]
];

Result: the payload dropped from 5.8 MB to 545 KB, a 90.6% reduction. Page load reconstructs the full search structure in about 32.9 ms, and the app no longer depends on a remote dataset fetch to become usable.

Phase 5: The AI counselor that failed, and why MCP was the right pivot

I tried to put a direct chatbot inside the app. It failed more often than I’m comfortable admitting. The issue wasn’t that the model was bad — it was that the domain was too structured, too quota-heavy, and too easy to hallucinate if the model had to carry the rules from memory.

So I stopped asking the model to be the source of truth.

Instead, I moved the hard logic into a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. That changed the architecture in a good way. AI assistants can now ask for exact cutoffs, fee tables, document checklists, and discrete simulations without guessing. The model becomes an interface, not an oracle.

  • Web app: clean 1-click experience for students and parents
  • MCP server: structured access for AI workflows and advanced users
  • Result: fewer hallucinations, better reproducibility, and cleaner separation of concerns

This was the moment the project stopped feeling like a chatbot experiment and started feeling like a real system.

Phase 6: UX simplification was not cosmetic — it was the product

One of the biggest mistakes early on was trying to expose too much. The more fields we added, the less confident users felt. Families in a stressful admission cycle do not want to configure a simulator. They want an answer.

So the interface was stripped down aggressively:

  • Only NEET AIR and Telangana State Rank in the main viewport
  • Category, gender, domicile, and PwD moved into a collapsible advanced panel
  • A single high-confidence action instead of multiple competing controls
  • Dark, glassy, bento-style cards to keep dense data readable

That shift mattered more than any animation or visual polish. The app started feeling fast because the user no longer had to think about the machinery before getting an answer.

Phase 7: College ordering and the real-world seat matrix

The engine pre-orders Telangana colleges by a practical preference hierarchy, not just by prestige. Distance from Rajendranagar, Hyderabad is part of the mental model because it affects real decisions for families.

  • Government colleges first, then private category-A colleges
  • Top institutions like Osmania, Gandhi, and ESIC early in the list
  • Peripheral and district colleges arranged by travel distance
  • Private colleges included with annual fee context

That ordering sounds simple, but it’s what makes the simulator feel like a real counseling workflow instead of a generic rank-to-college lookup.

What we learned

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                            WHAT WE LEARNED BUILDING MSEAT                     |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| 1. Empathy drives UX: Students in high-stress admission cycles do not want    |
|    complex forms. A clean 1-click interface builds instant trust.             |
|                                                                               |
| 2. Client-side simulation is powerful: Packing 18,000+ candidates into 545 KB |
|    gives users instant simulation with zero cloud server costs.               |
|                                                                               |
| 3. Data integrity is sacred: In medical admissions, a 1-mark discrepancy can  |
|    change a family's trajectory. Filtering outliers and verifying official    |
|    gazettes is essential.                                                     |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

If there’s one thing this project taught me, it’s that the hardest part of engineering is often not the algorithm — it’s the honesty required to admit when your algorithm is wrong. We started with a rank predictor that failed badly, then rebuilt the system around the actual rules, the actual data, and the actual stress users were carrying.

mSeat is still evolving, and that’s the right state for it to be in. The next steps with Vercel, Gemini/ChatGPT, and MCP are about making the system more accessible, more inspectable, and more useful to people who need answers fast. But the core lesson won’t change: in high-stakes systems, the truth has to be cheaper than the guess.

MCP: mseat.kprsnt.in/api/mcp
GitHub: github.com/kprsnt2/mSeat

🤖 AI View

I agree with the author’s core thesis: in a high-stakes domain like medical admissions, deterministic rules should own the truth, and AI should only assist around the edges. The pivot to MCP is especially strong because it reduces hallucination risk and gives the model a structured way to query verified logic instead of improvising answers. I also agree that UX simplification is not cosmetic here; it is part of the trust model. If anything, I’d push even harder on auditability and versioned data snapshots so users can see exactly which merit list and cutoff set produced a recommendation.
